Consult Summary:
- Telehealth consult for ongoing central chest pressure with dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, and left arm/shoulder radiation; ambulance activated for suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Aspirin allergy reported.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Central chest pressure “like someone sitting on chest,” began a couple of hours prior while gardening (not strenuous). Symptoms ongoing at time of call.
- Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea (no vomiting), left arm and shoulder pain. Reports heart beating faster now (palpitations today; not usually).
- Pertinent negatives: No prior similar episodes.
- Past medical history: Hypertension. No diabetes. Cholesterol has never been checked.
- Allergies: Aspirin—causes swelling (allergic reaction); described as mild and not life-threatening; patient has sometimes taken it despite mild reaction.
- Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction around age ~60; mother with heart problems (unspecified).
- Medications: Not discussed (not documented).
- Social history: Smokes ~10 cigarettes/day for 15 years. Alcohol ~7–8 pints of beer/week. Overweight (per patient). Sedentary activity level. Lives alone. Occupation: restaurant owner (sushi shop).

Examination:
- Vitals:
- Examination findings:

Impression:
- Suspected acute coronary syndrome (possible myocardial infarction) given ongoing central chest pressure with dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, and radiation to left arm/shoulder; multiple cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, smoking, family history, overweight).

Plan:
- Emergency response: Ambulance activated; clinician remained on the line until arrival.
- Safety: Advised to keep front door open for access.
- Prehospital assessment: EMS to perform ECG and determine destination based on findings.
- Medication considerations: Patient to clearly communicate aspirin allergy (swelling, mild, not life-threatening) to EMS/hospital; clinician noted aspirin may still be considered despite allergy, depending on risk/benefit.
- Disposition: EMS to transport to appropriate facility per ECG and clinical assessment.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Full medication list and antihypertensive regimen; vitals; physical exam; exact time of symptom onset; lipid profile/history; detailed family history for mother; past surgical history; vaccination status; advance directives.
- Internal conflicts: Minor ambiguity regarding palpitations—patient states heart is beating faster now due to stress and also that it doesn’t usually beat faster; interpreted as no baseline palpitations, present today.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor filler words and brief interruptions; no major inaudible sections.
